<reason>Both sides argued at a high level with clean structure, proper Q/A labels, and no fake sourcing. PRO won because it captured the decisive frame and kept it alive: it turned CON's own "targeted fixes" (detail-light EOBs, rerouted statements, intake lockdown) into an admission that the machinery of the motion is acceptable, narrowing the debate to default-vs-request, and then won that narrowed question with the burden-placement asymmetry ("privacy a confident adult can waive in a sentence, versus privacy a frightened one must earn by explaining herself to a stranger in ten minutes"). PRO also landed the best single counter to CON's alternatives: campus/cash-pay/sliding-scale options are "an affluence test dressed as an option," which CON answered only thinly (sliding scales scale with means; the deductible still moves). CON's strongest work was real and damaging — distinguishing reason-triggered confidentiality from age-keyed concealment, exposing that the second clause is about the payer's receipt rather than access, and the "payer paying blind / deductible moves with no matching claim" mechanic that PRO never fully resolved. Its Q1 extracted a genuine concession about clinics that bill nobody. But CON's early-warning-system pillar sits in tension with its own claim that the disclosed receipt is generic and harmless "nothing a dermatology visit wouldn't show": if the paperwork reveals almost nothing, it is a weak warning system, and if notification is what informs families, PRO's deterrence story bites. PRO's causal core (deterrence means no treatment, and confidentiality is the mechanism of therapy) survived contact. Execution cost against PRO: two turns clipped for exceeding the cap, though the lost text appears to be tails of points already made. Hence a clear but competitive win.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's [A2.1]-[A2.3] — "your targeted fixes *are* the motion" — reframed the whole debate and collapsed CON's fraud objection; CON's best recovery was [B2.1]/[B2.3], distinguishing reason-triggered requests from age-keyed default concealment and noting the deductible still moves, which kept CON alive but left PRO holding the cleaner decision rule on defaults.</best_rebuttal>
